etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English mad, madde, madd, medd, from Old English ġemǣdd, ġemǣded (“enraged”), past participle of ġemǣdan, *mǣdan (“to make insane or foolish”), from Proto-Germanic *maidijaną (“to change; damage; cripple; injure; make mad”), from Proto-Germanic *maidaz ("weak; crippled"; compare Old English gemād (“silly, mad”), Old High German gimeit (“foolish, crazy”), literary German gemeit (“mad, insane”), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌼𐌰𐌹𐌸𐍃 (gamaiþs, “crippled”)), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- ("to change"; compare Old Irish máel (“bald, dull”), Old Lithuanian ap-maitinti (“to wound”), Sanskrit मेथति (méthati, “he hurts, comes to blows”)).

definitions.definition: (chiefly British Isles) Insane; crazy, mentally deranged.

quote.citation: c. 1588–1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: I have heard my grandsire say full oft, / Extremity of griefs would make men mad.

quote.citation: 1920 October, Agatha Christie, “The Arrest”, in The Mysterious Affair at Styles […], New York, N.Y.: Grosset & Dunlap, published March 1927, page 218:
quote.text: Sometimes, I feel sure he is as mad as a hatter; and then, just as he is at his maddest, I find there is method in his madness.

quote.citation: 2008, BioWare, Mass Effect (Science Fiction), Redwood City: Electronic Arts, →ISBN, →OCLC, PC, scene: Eden Prime:
quote.text: Dr. Manuel: Is it madness to see the future? To see the destruction rushing towards us? To understand there is no escape? No hope? No, I am not mad. I'm the only sane one left!

definitions.definition: (chiefly US; informal in UK and Ireland) Angry, annoyed.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 26:11:
quote.text: And I punished them oft in euery Synagogue, and compelled them to blaspheme, and being exceedingly mad against them, I persecuted them euen vnto strange cities.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VI, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: She was so mad she wouldn't speak to me for quite a spell, but at last I coaxed her into going up to Miss Emmeline's room and fetching down a tintype of the missing Deacon man.

definitions.definition: (chiefly in the negative, informal) Used litotically to indicate satisfaction or approval.

quote.citation: 2019, The Real Housewives of Atlanta‎[1], season 13, episode 3:
quote.text: I'm not mad at this little house, though.

quote.citation: 2019, “'Thank U' Text: Ariana Grande's Collaborators Break Down The Artist's Latest Album”, in NPR‎[2]:
quote.text: But I mean, once the flow was there, nobody was mad at it.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Jeremiah 1:88:
quote.text: It is the land of graven images, and they are mad upon their idols.

quote.citation: 1787, R. Bage, The Fair Syrian, page 314:
quote.text: My brother, quiet as a cat, seems perfectly contented with the internal feelings of his felicity. The Marquis, mad as a kitten, is all in motion to express it, from tongue to heel.

quote.citation: 2010 May 27, Judy Astley, Blowing It: a brilliantly funny, mad-cap novel guaranteed to make you laugh from bestselling author Judy Astley, Random House, →ISBN, page 287:
quote.text: […]  at all, just a vast space of desert out in the saltlands of Nevada. It's serious dressing up, the maddest entertainment, craziest art, and at the end there's the burning of a huge effigy, stuffed with pyrotechnics 287.

definitions.definition: Extremely foolish or unwise; irrational; imprudent.
(colloquial, usually with for or about) Extremely enthusiastic about; crazy about; infatuated with; overcome with desire for.
(of animals) Abnormally ferocious or furious; or, rabid, affected with rabies.
(slang, chiefly New York, African-American Vernacular) Intensifier, signifying abundance or high quality of a thing; very, much or many.
(of a compass needle) Having impaired polarity.
(slang, chiefly New York, African-American Vernacular, UK and Ireland, dialectal) Intensifier; to a large degree; extremely; exceedingly; very; unbelievably.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English madden, from the adjective; compare Old English ġemǣdan.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To be or become mad. [14th–19th c.]

quote.citation: 1832, Tales of the Alhambra, Washington Irving:
quote.text: The imperial Elizabetta gazed with surprise at the youthful and unpretending appearance of the little being that had set the world madding.

definitions.definition: (now colloquial US, Jamaica) To madden, to anger, to frustrate. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene 5]:
quote.text: This musick mads me, let it sound no more.

quote.citation: 1624, Democritus Junior [pseudonym; Robert Burton], The Anatomy of Melancholy: […], 2nd edition, Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  John Lichfield and James Short, for Henry Cripps, →OCLC, partition I, section 2, member 4, subsection iv:
quote.text: He that mads others, if he were so humoured, would be as mad himself, as much grieved and tormented  […] .

quote.citation: 1993 March 22, “Oh Carolina”, in Pure Pleasure‎[3], performed by Shaggy (musician):
quote.text: Carolina! Whine your body gyal! Make Dem know say you have it fi mad dem
